title: Ayurveda Day 2024: Embracing innovation for global health and sustainable wellness
summary: Ayurveda, an ancient system of medicine from India, emphasises holistic health by balancing the body, mind, and spirit. The word “Ayurveda” combines two Sanskrit terms: “ayu” (life) and “veda” (knowledge), translating to “knowledge of life.” In India, the Government has celebrated Ayurveda Day on Dhanawantari Jayanti (Dhanteras) annually since 2016 to promote awareness of Ayurvedic principles, medicinal plants, and lifestyle practices. This day is dedicated to Lord Dhanvantari, revered as the divine physician who brought this knowledge to humanity from Lord Brahma. Celebrating Ayurveda Day honors his contributions, highlighting Ayurveda’s core philosophies and health practices. On the occasion of Dhanvantari Jayanti and the 9th Ayurveda Day, Prime Minister Narendra Modi is set to inaugurate a series of significant health sector projects valued at over Rs 12,850 crore. These initiatives underscore India’s dedication to fostering accessible healthcare and promoting Ayurveda, a traditional system of medicine. A central part of this expansion is the second phase of the All India Institute of Ayurveda (AIIA), which now includes a Panchakarma hospital, an Ayurvedic pharmacy, a sports medicine unit, a central library, an IT and start-ups incubation center, and a 500-seat auditorium. Highlighting Ayurveda’s potential to complement modern medicine, PM Modi will also unveil four Ayush Centres of Excellence. These include the Centre of Excellence for diabetes and metabolic disorders at the Indian Institute of Science, Bengaluru, and the Centre of Excellence in sustainable Ayush for advanced technological solutions and start-up support at IIT Delhi. Additionally, the Central Drug Research Institute in Lucknow will host a Centre of Excellence for fundamental and translational research in Ayurveda, and Jawaharlal Nehru University in New Delhi will feature a Centre of Excellence on Ayurveda and Systems Medicine. Each center is committed to leveraging Ayurveda to address contemporary health issues while fostering sustainable healthcare solutions. The Prime Minister will also lay the foundation stones for two Central Research Institutes in Yoga and Naturopathy, located in Khordha, Odisha, and Raipur, Chhattisgarh. These initiatives are key steps in integrating Ayurveda into mainstream healthcare, strengthening research and clinical practice in traditional medicine, and showcasing Ayurveda’s significant role in India’s healthcare landscape. Ayurveda’s Role in Addressing Global Health Challenges Ayurveda, a centuries-old system of medicine, is increasingly being recognized for its potential to address complex global health issues. The theme “Ayurveda Innovation for Global Health” brings focus to how Ayurvedic approaches can provide sustainable and effective solutions, especially for combating non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and antimicrobial resistance. NCDs, like heart disease, diabetes, and cancer, are growing concerns worldwide, affecting millions and imposing a heavy economic burden. Ayurveda’s emphasis on individualized treatment and natural remedies provides an alternative pathway to managing these chronic conditions, with fewer side effects and more sustainable long-term health benefits. Tackling Health Challenges of Climate Change, Aging, and Mental Health The impact of climate change on health is undeniable, with increased respiratory illnesses, mental health strain, and a rise in infectious diseases. Ayurvedic practices promote natural harmony and resilience, equipping people to better handle these challenges. Ayurveda also emphasizes geriatric care, offering solutions to age-related ailments through personalized wellness plans. Furthermore, mental health support in Ayurveda—grounded in practices like yoga, meditation, and herbal therapies—can aid in managing stress, anxiety, and other mental health conditions, encouraging a holistic approach to psychological well-being. Emphasising Preventive Health and Holistic Wellness Preventive health lies at the core of Ayurveda, aligning well with the global shift toward holistic wellness. Ayurveda’s preventive focus encourages lifestyle modifications, diet management, and routine health practices to maintain balance and prevent illness before it arises. Such measures are particularly important in reducing the global health burden by decreasing the prevalence of lifestyle-related diseases. The integration of Ayurveda into preventive health care can thus play a pivotal role in achieving long-term wellness. Supporting SDGs and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) In alignment with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Universal Health Coverage (UHC), Ayurveda offers a framework that promotes equity, accessibility, and affordability in health care. Its low-cost, low-tech interventions can reach underserved populations, helping bridge the gap in health equity. Ayurveda’s integration into global health systems aligns with SDG targets for ensuring healthy lives and promoting well-being for all, paving the way for a more inclusive and sustainable health care model globally. The theme “Ayurveda Innovation for Global Health” underscores the potential of Ayurvedic approaches in addressing modern health challenges. By embracing its preventive, holistic, and inclusive principles, Ayurveda can make a meaningful contribution to global health and well-being. Understanding the 2024 Theme: “Ayurveda Innovation for Global Health” This year’s theme, “Ayurveda Innovation for Global Health,” highlights the vital role Ayurvedic medicine can play in addressing pressing health challenges worldwide. By embracing innovation within the traditional Ayurvedic system, the focus is on addressing contemporary health issues through a holistic, preventive, and sustainable approach. This theme supports initiatives like combatting non-communicable diseases (NCDs) and antimicrobial resistance, recognizing the urgent need for sustainable healthcare solutions. Additionally, Ayurveda’s unique emphasis on balancing mind, body, and environment aligns with the rising global interest in addressing climate change, geriatric care, mental health, and nutritional disorders holistically. This focus on preventive health and holistic wellness also connects deeply with the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs) and Universal Health Coverage (UHC) vision, emphasizing accessible, affordable, and effective healthcare for all. Ayurveda’s integration into the global health framework presents an opportunity to innovate traditional practices and bring them into modern contexts, fostering improved quality of life worldwide. summary: Ash gourd, also known as winter melon or white pumpkin, is a tropical fruit that is often overlooked in many diets. Despite its humble appearance and mild flavour, ash gourd is packed with essential nutrients and offers numerous health benefits. Rich in water content, vitamins, and minerals, this versatile vegetable has been a staple in traditional medicine for centuries. This article explores the many health benefits of ash gourd and why you should consider adding it to your daily diet. Rich in nutrients and low in calories Ash gourd is low in calories but high in nutritional value, making it an excellent choice for anyone looking to maintain a healthy weight. A 100-gram serving of ash gourd provides only around 13 calories, making it a guilt-free option for weight management. It is also a good source of dietary fibre, vitamins like vitamin C, and minerals such as calcium, iron, and potassium. These nutrients help support overall health and well-being. Supports hydration With its high water content (about 96%), ash gourd is a great food for staying hydrated. Hydration is essential for various bodily functions, including digestion, temperature regulation, and skin health. Consuming foods with high water content, like ash gourd, can help you maintain fluid balance, particularly during hot weather or after exercise. Aids in digestion Ash gourd is rich in dietary fibre, which aids in the smooth functioning of the digestive system. Fibre helps in preventing constipation by promoting regular bowel movements and improving overall gut health. Additionally, ash gourd contains compounds that help soothe the stomach lining, making it beneficial for those suffering from gastric issues or acid reflux. Boosts immune health The high vitamin C content in ash gourd plays a key role in boosting the immune system. Vitamin C is known to enhance the production of white blood cells, which help fight infections and protect the body from harmful pathogens. Consuming ash gourd regularly can support your immune defence and reduce the risk of illnesses, especially during seasonal changes. Promotes healthy skin Ash gourd’s high water content and vitamin C make it excellent for maintaining healthy, glowing skin. Vitamin C is an antioxidant that helps protect the skin from free radicals, preventing premature ageing and the formation of wrinkles. The hydrating properties of ash gourd also help keep the skin moisturized, preventing dryness and promoting a smooth complexion. Supports weight loss Because of its low calorie and high water content, ash gourd is a perfect addition to a weight loss diet. It provides bulk to your meals, which helps you feel full without consuming excess calories. Moreover, its high fibre content helps regulate blood sugar levels, preventing sudden spikes and crashes that often lead to overeating. Regulates blood sugar levels Ash gourd has a low glycemic index, which means it has a minimal impact on blood sugar levels. This makes it an ideal food for people with diabetes or those looking to control their blood sugar levels. The fibre in ash gourd helps regulate the absorption of sugar, preventing sudden spikes in glucose levels after meals. Promotes Heart health The potassium content in ash gourd helps regulate blood pressure, reducing the risk of hypertension and heart disease. Additionally, the antioxidants present in ash gourd help lower cholesterol levels, improving overall cardiovascular health. Regular consumption of ash gourd can thus support heart health and reduce the risk of heart-related problems. Detoxifies the body Ash gourd is known for its detoxifying properties. It helps in flushing out toxins from the body by promoting urine production and cleansing the kidneys. Consuming ash gourd regularly can assist in removing waste from the system, aiding in detoxification and overall bodily function. Supports Respiratory health Ash gourd has been traditionally used in Ayurvedic medicine to treat respiratory issues like cough, asthma, and bronchitis. The fruit has anti-inflammatory properties that help clear the airways and ease breathing. It is also believed to have a cooling effect on the body, which can soothe irritation in the throat and lungs. Whether you’re looking to improve digestion, boost your immune system, manage your weight, or support heart and skin health, incorporating ash gourd into your diet can offer remarkable results. With its low-calorie count, rich nutrient profile, and versatile culinary uses, ash gourd is truly a superfood deserving of more attention.

Five minutes of daily exercise could reduce blood pressure
summary: Sydney: Exercising for five minutes per day could reduce blood pressure, a new research has found. The research, which was published by experts from an international academic collaboration led by the University of Sydney and University College London on Thursday, suggested that doing five minutes of physical activity, such as walking uphill or stair climbing every day may help to lower blood pressure. According to the study by the Prospective Physical Activity, Sitting and Sleep (ProPASS) Consortium, replacing sedentary behaviour with 20-27 minutes of exercise per day can result in a clinically meaningful reduction in blood pressure. "High blood pressure is one of the biggest health issues globally, but unlike some major causes of cardiovascular mortality there may be relatively accessible ways to tackle the problem in addition to medication," Emmanuel Stamatakis, joint senior author and director of the ProPASS Consortium from the University of Sydney, said. "The finding that doing as little as five extra minutes of exercise per day could be associated with measurably lower blood pressure readings emphasises how powerful short bouts of higher intensity movement could be for blood pressure management." The research team analysed data from 14,761 volunteers to see how replacing one type of movement with another is associated with blood pressure. The team estimated that replacing sedentary behaviour with at least 20 minutes of exercise daily could reduce cardiovascular disease incidence by 28 per cent. The World Health Organisation estimated that 1.28 billion adults aged 30-79 years worldwide have hypertension, consistent elevated blood pressure, and that 46 per cent of adults with hypertension are unaware they have the condition. (IANS)

summary: Wellington: New Zealand has declared early stages of a highly contagious whooping cough epidemic, with a nationally coordinated response now in place, the Ministry of Health said on Friday. New Zealand health officials have met to review the latest national and international trends in whooping cough, or pertussis, across the country, which have been closely monitored over recent months and can be particularly dangerous for newborn babies, and older adults, with three babies having died from whooping cough last year, Xinhua news agency reported.Case numbers consistently increased for several weeks across New Zealand, meeting the threshold for a national epidemic to be declared, a Ministry of Health statement said, citing the country's last major outbreak of pertussis in 2017, which lasted for months and potentially for a year or more.Whooping cough cases have been steadily increasing again since September, following spikes in May, June and July, according to the Institute of Environmental Science and Research.There were 263 cases in the past four weeks between October 19 and November 15 in New Zealand, the highest number of cases over a four-week period to date for all of 2024, it said.New Zealand should also be ready to see similarly high levels of cases over the next 12 months or more, as a number of countries are experiencing record levels of pertussis, possibly due to lower infection rates during the COVID-19 pandemic, said Nicholas Jones, director of public health at the Ministry of Health.Jones warned of the risk of severe illness among babies either too young to be immunised or whose immunisations are delayed, as well as Maori and Pacific people living in New Zealand who will be most affected."Even in countries with very high levels of immunisation, epidemics still occur every few years, but the number of babies who get very sick is much lower when mothers have been vaccinated during pregnancy, and when people are vaccinated on time," she said.(IANS)

title: Increased intake of plant protein to boost your heart health
summary: New Delhi: Eating more plant-based protein than animal-based protein may help reduce the risk of cardiovascular disease (CVD) and coronary heart disease (CHD), according to a new study on Monday. The study, led by researchers at Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, showed that the risk reductions are likely driven by the replacement of red and processed meats with plant proteins and eating more legumes and nuts.“Such a dietary pattern is beneficial not just for human health but also the health of our planet," they said in the study, published in the American Journal of Clinical Nutrition.The study aims to pioneer the investigation of an ideal ratio of plant to animal protein and how it impacts health, specifically heart health."The average American eats a 1:3 plant-to-animal protein ratio. Our findings suggest a ratio of at least 1:2 is much more effective in preventing CVD," said lead author Andrea Glenn, Assistant Professor in the Department of Nutrition and Food Studies at New York University. Glenn worked on the study as a postdoctoral fellow at Harvard Chan School.To prevent CHD, a ratio of 1:1.3 or higher should come from plants, Glenn said.The team used 30 years of data on diet, lifestyle, and heart health among nearly 203,000 men and women. Throughout the four-year study period, 16,118 CVD cases, including over 10,000 CHD cases and over 6,000 stroke cases, were documented.The results showed that people who consumed a higher ratio of plant to animal protein (about 1:1.3) had a 19 per cent lower risk of CVD and a 27 per cent lower risk of CHD.Further, people who had their 21 per cent of energy coming from proteins and adhered to a higher plant-to-animal protein ratio saw a 28 per cent lower risk of CVD and a 36 per cent lower risk of CHD.According to the researchers, replacing processed meat with several plant protein sources, particularly nuts and legumes can improve blood lipids and blood pressure as well as inflammatory biomarkers. It is partly because plant proteins are often accompanied by high amounts of fibre, antioxidant vitamins, minerals, and healthy fats.(IANS)

title: What Is The 'Bleeding Eye' Virus That Has Sparked Global Fear? Check Symptoms Of Deadly Marburg Disease
summary: The deadly Marburg virus disease (MVD) is reportedly on the spread in Africa, claiming 15 lives in Rwanda, and prompting countries like the US and the UK to issue warnings to its citizens planning to visit the continent. MVD, formerly known as Marburg hemorrhagic fever, and now as Bleeding Eye Virus, is a severe, often fatal illness in humans, according to the WHO.The UK Daily Mirror reports that the Marburg virus, which has a 50-50 chance of death and is thought to be one of the deadliest on earth, could soon spread after 15 people died in Rwanda. UK Health authorities have issued a warning to its citizens after hundreds more have reported to have been infected with the disease, and there is likelihood that other African countries could see cases too. No cases have been reported inside India as yet. The scare has elicited heightened vigilance at US airports. In September, the CNN reported that for the first time in Rwanda’s history, its health ministry was dealing with an outbreak of Marburg virus disease, a rare but deadly haemorrhagic disease similar to Ebola. What makes it deadlier than Ebola is that there is no treatment or vaccines for Marburg, and it has a fatality rate of 88 per cent.In October, the US Department of Health and Human Services declared that while the outbreak of Marburg virus in Rwanda rages on, travellers coming into the United States who have been in Rwanda in the previous 21 days will be screened starting mid of the month.Moreover, the continuous spread of Mpox and Oropouche in several countries has also triggered fear among travellers. The US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention began public health entry screening to reduce the risk of the importation and spread of cases.Reports say that the Mpox clade 1 strains have also been detected in Burundi, Central African Republic, Democratic Republic of Congo, Gabon, Uganda and Kenya. This year, the UK has had five confirmed instances of the more serious of the Mpox cases, which were previously limited to just five nations in central Africa.The most recent case was a patient who just returned from Uganda, and was announced in Leeds on Sunday. The first had returned from Africa on October 21 and the other four lived in the same London household.There is no pre-travel mpox vaccine, and therefore the UK government has advised its citizens to consult their doctors before departing the country to determine their suitability for travel. Travel Health Pro, an information website commissioned by the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA), has posted: “In particular, pregnant and immunosuppressed people are known to be at higher risk of severe infection. Check your travel health insurance before you go.”Bleeding Eye Virus: Who Should Be Vigilant?Pregnant womenImmunocompromised individuals Transplant patientsAutoimmune disorder patientsThose on immune-suppression drugsPatients battling cancerDiabeticsThese patients may run a higher risk of severe infection.Bleeding Eye Virus Symptoms The Metro UK website credits the World Health Organization for information that the Marburg virus once inside a person’s body may undergo an incubation period of two to 21 days, and the first symptoms of Marburg disease start abruptly. Initial symptoms manifested are:feversevere headachessevere malaisemuscle aches and painsSymptoms that emerge on the third day:severe watery diarrhoeaabdominal pain and crampingnauseavomitingnon-itchy rashDay Five symptoms include:fresh blood in vomit and faecesbleeding from the nose, gums, vagina, eyes, mouth and earsinternal bleedingconfusionirritabilityaggressioninflammation of the testiclesPatients have a high chance of losing the battle against this deadly disease and may die eight or nine days after symptoms start, often due to the blood loss or shock syndrome, reports Metro.co.uk. MVD is referred to as the "bleeding eye" virus because it damages the blood vessels, causing people to bleed from various orifices, including eyes.What Tests Are Done To Confirm Bleeding Eye Virus?According to the WHO, it can be difficult to clinically distinguish MVD from other infectious diseases such as malaria, typhoid fever, shigellosis, meningitis and other viral haemorrhagic fevers. The WHO website says that the confirmation that symptoms are caused by Marburg virus infection are made using the following diagnostic methods:antibody-capture enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA)antigen-capture detection testsreverse transcriptase polymerase chain reaction (RT-PCR) assayvirus isolation by cell culture in maximum containment laboratories.The author is an independent journalist.
